name: Heroes of Legend · Dungeon Architect’s Guide & Bestiary

text.content:
Becoming the Dungeon Architect

Heroes of Legend · Dungeon Architect’s Guide & Bestiary

Rain runs down the broken gate. Beyond it, a lantern moves where no living guard should stand. One hero reaches for a weapon; another recognizes the lantern's signal. You describe the light, answer their questions, and ask what they do. Their answer is where the adventure begins.

As the Dungeon Architect, or DA, you portray the world beyond the heroes. You give its inhabitants purposes, reveal what the characters can perceive, and apply the rules when an uncertain choice has consequences. The players decide what their heroes attempt. Together, your decisions turn a prepared situation into a story none of you could have written alone.

You do not need to prepare every road beyond the gate. You need to know who holds the lantern, what they want, and what might happen when someone answers it.

A world worth entering

Give the players something they can act upon. A ruined watchtower becomes useful when its beacon is still burning, someone is trapped beneath it, and the only visible stairs have collapsed. Describe a few distinct details, then let questions bring the rest into focus. A smell of wet ash or a voice behind the wall can do more work than a page of history.

Tell players what their characters would reasonably know. A local knows which bridge charges a toll. A healer recognizes ordinary signs of injury. A hero standing beside a roaring furnace can feel its heat. Do not hide obvious danger behind a roll, or withhold ordinary knowledge until someone uses the right phrase. Specialist abilities matter when the task calls for their expertise or their printed benefits.

Make consequences follow established circumstances. A guard who heard shouting may investigate. A merchant whose stock was saved may offer favorable terms. Once the group learns these connections, preparation and clever choices become useful. They can trust that a door stays unlocked after they unlock it.

Before the first session

Bring the players into the conversation before they finish their characters. Describe the kind of adventures you intend to offer: expeditions into forgotten places, dangerous roads, struggles between rival powers, or some mixture. Ask what each hero hopes to accomplish and why these people would travel together. A shared debt, a rescue, a commission or a promise can bring very different heroes onto the same road.

Discuss the game's lasting injuries and death. HP can return after a safe breath; spent Grit and wounds remain. Agree on how much detail the group wants when those injuries occur. A player can prefer a brief statement of a wound's effects without changing those effects. Establish a simple way for anyone to pause or redirect a scene when its content makes play uncomfortable.

Set practical expectations as well: session length, attendance, how the group handles an absent player, and whether players enjoy speaking in character or summarizing their intent. Both approaches work. A player's confidence as a speaker should not determine whether their silver-tongued hero gets to use an ability.

PrepareA useful first-session answer
A shared reason to actSomeone the heroes care about is overdue at a nearby crossing.
A place to beginA crowded ferry house with news, supplies and a disputed map.
A visible problemThe crossing's signal has changed, and the ferryman refuses to sail.
People with different wantsOne wants a rescue; another wants the road reopened quietly.
Several approachesFollow the bank, bargain for passage, or inspect the old causeway.
A possible oppositionA few creature cards whose motives fit the place.
A consequence of delayThe stranded travelers move to a less safe shelter.

This is enough to begin. Keep the names, nearby locations and creature cards within reach. Leave room to discover what the players consider important.

The rhythm of Heroes of Legend

HOL puts much of its strategy into character development. At the table, a player chooses an action, declares the card they are using before the roll, and follows its result. Your job is to establish the circumstances that make those choices interesting: a narrow escape, a crowded bridge, an ally who needs a free hand.

Attacks always hit. Defensive play changes the outcome and the damage suffered; it does not create a routine miss. Since damage is only part of an attack, pay attention to the push that opens a route, the condition that changes a plan, or the maneuver that allows someone else to act safely.

A safe breath restores HP. This lets the next encounter begin with heroes ready to act, while wounds and spent Grit preserve the cost of earlier danger. Do not assume a campaign needs a fixed number of fights between rests. An encounter can matter because it costs time, exposes a secret, changes an alliance, or leaves a scar, even when everyone later returns to full HP.

Share the spotlight

Watch who is making decisions. After one player negotiates with the watch captain, turn to the scout studying the courtyard or the healer tending a frightened witness. Invite a contribution without requiring every hero to roll in every scene. Sometimes the right contribution is a question or a choice to trust a companion.

Read the characters' less frequently used cards during preparation. Put opportunities for them in the world: tracks worth following, a wound that needs proper treatment, an object whose history can be discovered. Present the opportunity clearly. A player should not need to guess that you prepared a scene for their expertise.

Let a good plan work. If the heroes bring the documents an official needs, obtain permission and take the safe road, do not move the ambush onto that road merely to preserve a fight. Preparation earns its value through what it changes.

When the unexpected happens

Pause long enough to understand the plan. Determine whether it can work, whether an existing card covers it, and what makes its outcome uncertain. If the players have solved the problem through their actions, describe the result. If danger or uncertainty remains, establish the stakes and call for the appropriate roll.

You can make a consistent ruling without designing a permanent subsystem. Explain it briefly, apply it to comparable situations, and note a question for later review if it is likely to recur. If a mistaken ruling materially changes a player's decision, offer to revisit that decision before proceeding.

Close the session with something to carry forward

Ask what the heroes intend to do next. Record people helped or harmed, promises, new information, treasure and unresolved threats. Confirm wounds, treatment progress, Grit and supplies with the players. Their plans tell you what to prepare; the consequences tell you what the world does while they prepare.

For a first outing, @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.da-rules.JournalEntry.fcfeb03f877503a3.JournalEntryPage.f57043a66e0f2721]{The Bell at the Crossing} provides a small place, a solvable problem and several people with reasons to care. Use it whole or borrow the pieces that suit your table.

Running the Game

Heroes of Legend · Dungeon Architect’s Guide & Bestiary

A player wants to slip past a watchman, pull a companion from a river, or convince a frightened witness to speak. Begin with the intended action. The dice enter when you know what is uncertain and why the answer matters.

The following procedure works in a crowded market as readily as in a dungeon. Existing cards take precedence where they provide a specific action and outcome.

From intent to consequence

Ask what the hero wants and how they attempt it. Establish what they can perceive, what their action can accomplish, and what happens if they make only limited progress. Give the player this information before they commit. They may choose a different approach once they understand the risk.

If the action plainly works, let it work. Lifting a rug reveals the trapdoor beneath it. Walking across a sound bridge does not require a balance roll. If an attempt cannot work, explain the obstacle: the gate is beyond reach, the witness does not know the answer, or the chosen ability cannot target what the hero cannot see.

When uncertainty carries a consequence, call for an attribute or use the attribute printed on the declared card. The six attributes are Brawn, Fortitude, Agility, Guile, Knowledge and Reason. Do not add a skill bonus or replace an ability's attribute because another attribute is stronger. A Force action calls for Brawn; “Force” is not a seventh kind of roll.

A player declares a card before rolling. Afterward, resolve the chosen action's outcome. An unexpected low result is not permission to switch to another card.

Difficulty without changing the target

Roll 3d6 plus the named attribute. Weak is 8 or below, Standard is 9–14, and Strong is 15 or above. Difficulty changes the dice through Boons and Banes, not these thresholds.

Boons and Banes cancel one for one. Roll one extra die for each remaining Boon or Bane, to a maximum of three extra dice. With Boons, keep the highest three; with Banes, keep the lowest three. Add the attribute to those three dice. Three retained natural 1s produce Weak plus a complication; three retained natural 6s produce Strong plus a benefit.

Use a single Bane for a meaningful obstacle, two for a severe obstacle and three for an exceptional obstacle that remains possible. Apply Boons in the same way for useful advantages. These descriptions help you make consistent judgments; they do not turn an impossible action into a difficult roll. Do not count the same circumstance twice under different names.

> Example: the rain-slick ledge. A hero follows a narrow ledge under pressure. > You assign 1 Bane for its slippery footing. An ally supplies plausible Aid for > 1 Boon. They cancel, leaving the ordinary three dice. The ledge does not also > change Standard to 12 or add an extra numerical penalty.

Weak is progress

A consequence is what the action puts at stake. A complication introduces an additional problem without taking away progress already earned. A benefit adds an advantage. State the ordinary outcome before rolling; add a complication or benefit when the rules or the circumstances call for one.

An ability already tells you what its Weak, Standard and Strong results do. Do not replace Weak damage with a miss, or substitute an invented drawback for the card's printed result. Outside a card's specific procedure, agree on what progress means in the current situation.

> Example: persuade the ferryman. The ferryman refuses to cross while the bell > at the far landing sounds an alarm. A hero asks him to reveal what he saw. You > establish that Weak gets an account from shore, Standard persuades him to guide > them along the bank, and Strong also earns the use of his boat once the alarm is > resolved. The roll cannot make him know who rang the bell. A natural 111 might > add that another listener reports the conversation; his account remains gained.

If another attempt would be identical and could be repeated without cost, danger or change, summarize the work instead of asking for rolls until someone gets Strong. Where an attempt consumes meaningful time, state how much time and what may change. Let a new approach change the circumstances rather than charging a roll simply for the privilege of trying again.

Information, perception and hiding

Describe obvious information freely. When a consequential search is uncertain, call for Reason. When someone might perceive a concealed player character, that player rolls Agility to remain Hidden. Do not add an opposed observer roll. A hidden hero needs plausible concealment; a good die result cannot hide them in an empty, brightly lit room.

Hidden is a universal state. Do not maintain a separate hidden marker for each observer. Attacking or openly revealing oneself ends it. Judge movement by the actual concealment available. Invisible prevents sight but does not necessarily conceal location: footprints in ash, a ringing bell or a moving curtain still matter. Active searching or attempting to hide during combat costs a Main Action unless a card says otherwise.

For an unscripted search or concealment roll, say what each outcome can achieve in that scene. Do not assume every Weak search finds nothing, or that every Weak stealth roll grants Hidden. It might reveal the direction of a sound while leaving its source unknown, or reach shelter while leaving a visible trail. These are scene rulings, not new universal outcome tables.

Never put every route to an essential clue behind one roll. If players inspect the thing that contains the answer, give them the answer. Other rolls can determine how quickly they understand it, what else they discover, or who notices them.

Work together outside combat

A group check combines several heroes' efforts outside combat. Name the task, who can meaningfully contribute, its target, the time per attempt and its consequence. State whether the task is binary, which must reach its target in one attempt, or cumulative, which retains progress between attempts.

Each participant rolls an appropriate attribute and contributes 1/2/3 progress on Weak/Standard/Strong. A hero can contribute their own roll or provide Aid to another participant, not both to the same attempt. Set the target for the actual task and space available. Do not quietly raise it whenever another helper joins.

> Example: the gate before the patrol. Three heroes can get a shoulder beneath > the swollen gate. The task is binary, target 7, one attempt before the patrol > rounds the bend. Weak, Standard and Strong total 6: the gate stays closed and the > patrol arrives. Weak, Strong and Strong total 7: it opens. The 6 does not carry > into the next attempt. Hauling a boulder uphill could instead retain its progress > because the task is cumulative.

A three-person attempt yields 3–9 progress before special effects. Use that range to avoid accidentally assigning an unreachable target. A target represents the amount of combined work, not a new difficulty threshold for each roll. Group checks do not apply to combat, crafting, recipe derivation or wound treatment. In combat, a hero can spend their own Force action on an obstacle under its normal rules; the group does not pool simultaneous rolls.

Conversation is an action in the world

Give an NPC a want, a concern and a limit. Let the players speak in character or summarize a proposal. Use the attribute printed on a social card. Without one, choose the attribute that matches the approach: Guile for a deceptive bargain, Knowledge for a technical case, or Reason to untangle conflicting accounts.

Good evidence may settle a question without a roll. A roll can change how a witness cooperates, but cannot make them reveal a fact they never knew. Likewise, a bargain does not erase another person's responsibilities or compel a player character's beliefs. Apply an explicit supernatural ability according to its card; ordinary persuasion does not acquire that ability by a high result.

> Example: the missing wage chest. A guard suspects the heroes of theft. Showing > the recovered chest and its unbroken seal answers that suspicion. Do not require > a second persuasion roll just to make the guard notice the seal. Negotiating > access to a restricted archive afterward is a different request.

Enter turns when order matters

Use combat turns when competing actions, immediate danger and short durations need an exact order. At the start, roll unmodified 3d6 once: 12 or above means the players' side starts; below 12 means the opposing side starts. Alternate one actor from each side. Each side chooses its next actor. When one side has no unacted members, the other finishes its remaining turns. The same side starts each round; do not reroll initiative.

Each actor has one Main Action, one Maneuver, one Reaction and movement. Main converts to Maneuver, and Maneuver to movement; conversion never goes upward. An ordinary defense roll does not spend the defender's Reaction. A shield hunker or an opportunity attack does.

Starting a provoking action triggers an available opportunity attack before that action resolves. It uses Basic Melee, not a specialty card. Resolve it, then continue the original action if its actor remains capable. Damage alone does not cancel a spell or other action. Leaving melee voluntarily, casting beside an enemy, standing, stowing and retrieving items can provoke. Forced movement does not. Drawing a weapon as part of its attack remains part of that action.

> Example: a healer under pressure. A hero next to an enemy begins casting a > healing spell. The enemy spends its Reaction on Basic Melee. If the hero remains > capable and can pay the healing cost while staying above 0 HP, the spell proceeds. > If the attack drops the hero to 0, they cannot continue. There is no extra > concentration or counterspell roll.

Who handles the dice

SituationRoll and result
A player character attacksThe player rolls the attack; read attack outcomes. Even against another PC, do not add a defense roll.
A creature attacks a PCThe player rolls the named defense attribute; read the creature's defense outcomes.
A creature uses an area attack against PCsEach affected player rolls their own defense.
A player uses an area attackRoll once using the worst applicable target modifiers.
A player-controlled summon acts or defendsIts controller rolls the summon's printed attribute and uses the appropriate player reference.
An NPC attacks an NPCA player or the DA assuming that role rolls the defender's named attribute; read the attacker's defense outcomes.
An NPC heals or performs another consequential taskA player or the DA rolls the acting NPC's printed attribute and outcomes.

Apply ordinary modifiers in each case. Rolling for an NPC does not transfer control of that NPC. Events well away from the heroes can be resolved by your judgment without simulating a battle nobody is playing.

Return to the scene

When immediate opposition ends, resolve remaining urgent consequences before moving on. A Dying character still needs their survival procedure. Burning can be put out when companions have the time and means to do so; combat need not continue merely to count safe, uncontested extinguishing actions. A lasting wound, curse or persistent condition remains until its own remedy applies.

Once the heroes can safely take a breath, restore full HP. Preserve Grit expenditure, scars and other continuing effects. Ask what they do with the scene they have changed: whom they help, what they search, and whether they stay or leave.

Building Adventures

Heroes of Legend · Dungeon Architect’s Guide & Bestiary

An adventure begins with something that cannot stay as it is. A bridge has closed, a tomb has opened, or two allies have made promises that cannot both be kept. Give the heroes a reason to care and a chance to change the outcome.

Prepare the people, places and pressures around that problem. Leave the heroes' solutions to their players. A useful adventure can survive a bargain you did not expect, an avoided fight, or a villain captured before delivering a speech.

Start with the problem

Write one sentence naming what is wrong and who is affected. Then write what happens if nobody intervenes. These statements give the adventure direction without deciding the players' actions.

“The village is threatened by monsters” gives you little to run. “The quarry has broken into an occupied burial hall, and its guardians now prevent the workers from reaching the only road out” gives you people, a place, a cause and several possible solutions. The heroes might close the breach, learn the guardians' orders, find another road or fight their way through.

Give the problem a visible face. A frightened apprentice arrives with a broken lantern. The ferryman has tied his boat ashore. An old rival asks for help and cannot afford to be proud. The opening should invite a decision the players can make with the information they have.

Offer reasons, not a single hook

Tie the situation to more than one interest. Coin can draw one hero; a missing friend draws another; a rare recipe interests a third. Ask players where their characters connect to the problem. Their answers can replace a disposable employer with someone the company already cares about.

Keep the offered terms clear. If a patron promises payment, say what counts as completion. “Return my brother alive” and “reopen the crossing” are different contracts. If those goals later conflict, that conflict should come from the situation, not from a hidden change to the agreement.

Make opposition want something

An adversary's purpose tells you how they act when the plan goes wrong. A robber wants supplies. A sentinel preserves a boundary. A rival expedition wants credit for a discovery. These motives supply ways to bargain, distract, bypass or defeat them without inventing a special peaceful solution for every scene.

For each important adversary, note what they know, what they fear losing, and what would make them retreat or negotiate. An ancestry is not a motive. Two goblins may have different loyalties; a ghost may understand an offer a living guard rejects. Creature cards supply useful starting purposes and counterplay, not compulsory personalities for every individual.

Build places that connect

Sketch the adventure as connected locations before you draw detailed squares. A crossing might link a ferry house, an old causeway, a toll yard and a buried signal room. Give important places more than one route where the geography allows it. Decide which routes are obvious, which can be discovered, and what choosing each route costs in time, danger or access.

At each location, prepare a short arrival description, what is happening, what can be learned, and what changes when the heroes interfere. Add a battle map only where positioning might matter. Show exits, cover, obstacles and hazards clearly. A secret route should lead somewhere useful, not merely skip a paragraph.

Clues should connect the adventure

For every fact the heroes need, provide several plausible ways to learn it. A signal's meaning might appear in a keeper's log, in a diagram by the bell, and in the ferryman's memory. These are separate opportunities, not three required rolls.

Distinguish finding evidence from interpreting it. Reading a legible name does not need a roll. An identification card may reveal properties of an enchanted object that ordinary inspection cannot. A Reason roll under pressure may reveal a hurried alteration before the author returns. Give each procedure the work it actually does.

If the heroes miss a clue, let the world continue. Another witness may approach, the threat may expose itself, or the group may choose a less informed route. Preserve what their earlier decisions changed. Do not silently move every missed clue into the next room until only one interpretation is possible.

Pressure you can explain

Choose events that follow from time or action. A caravan leaves at dusk. Water reaches a weakened foundation after the rain. A lookout runs for help if allowed to escape. Tell the players what their heroes can recognize about these dangers.

Use a short sequence of likely developments, not a secret timer that advances whenever you want tension. If the heroes stop the messenger, the reinforcements should not arrive by an unexplained alternative route. If an event's timing is uncertain, decide and record it before the choice that depends upon it.

PressureVisible signA way to change it
Workers prepare to abandon a siteCarts are being loaded; a foreman announces departure.Secure the road or persuade them a workable rescue is underway.
A rival takes the same routeFamiliar bootprints cross the fresh mud.Travel faster, negotiate, or choose another entrance.
A dangerous machine keeps operatingIts cycle is audible and its controls are visible.Stop its power, operate the controls, or pass during a safe interval.
A captive is being movedA witness reports preparations and the destination.Intercept the transfer or arrange access at its destination.

Mix the kinds of choices

An investigation needs people who know different parts of the truth. A rescue needs a person in danger and a route that can carry them out. An expedition needs places worth discovering and a reason to choose one route over another. A siege needs supplies, loyalties and exits as well as enemies.

Look at your party's abilities when deciding what those places contain. A tracker needs readable signs. A negotiator needs someone able to agree. A crafter needs materials, recipes or damaged objects worth understanding. Give these opportunities real consequences; do not confine utility abilities to decorative scenes between important fights.

Let an ability bypass a problem it is designed to solve. A hero who invested in that capability should feel the difference. The rest of the adventure can respond to their success without taking it away.

End with a changed situation

An adventure can finish when the crossing opens, the prisoner is safe, or the truth becomes public. It need not finish with every opponent dead. Settle promised rewards, show who benefited, and ask what the heroes do with what they learned.

Record unresolved elements as future possibilities: the employer who lied, the rival spared, the recipe found without its rare ingredient. Avoid turning every success into a concealed disaster. A rescued person can simply be grateful.

The following adventure demonstrates these tools in a small area. Its names, architecture and local customs can change without changing its central problem.

The Bell at the Crossing

Heroes of Legend · Dungeon Architect’s Guide & Bestiary

A bell sounds across a misty river. Each time it rings, the ferryman pulls his boat farther onto the bank. The travelers stranded at his shelter have begun arguing about the old causeway. Nobody agrees on what the signal means.

This short adventure suits a company beginning at level 1. Its possible fights use existing creature cards and provisional CV totals; those totals are not a promise of difficulty. Read the party's actual capabilities before play. The adventure can be resolved without fighting, and its locations can occupy one session or expand into several.

Names, placements, rewards and obstacle targets belong to this adventure. They do not establish universal rules.

What happened

The far landing stands above an older guard station. Two salvage workers opened its sealed signal room and disturbed three Skeleton Sentries whose final command was to keep strangers beyond the painted threshold. One worker, Nera, escaped into the bell loft. Her companion Tovin is hiding in a stores alcove outside that threshold. Both are alive when the adventure begins.

A small bandit crew has occupied the toll yard above the landing. They claim that the bell signals a deadly plague and demand payment for passage along the causeway. Their leader, Brin, knows there is no plague. Brin has heard the sentries but has not entered their chamber. The crew wants money and a way out before the district's road wardens arrive.

The ferryman, Oren, knows the bell's old rescue signal. What he hears is close to that signal but irregular. He fears rowing passengers into an ambush. Mara, a carrier with goods stranded across the river, offers the company 80 coins total to restore safe access and bring any survivors out. The agreement does not require them to kill anyone. Food and a dry place in Oren's shelter are available while they investigate.

People to portray

PersonWhat the heroes noticeWant and limit
Oren, ferrymanChecks the boat's knots whenever the bell sounds.Wants proof that the landing is safe; will share his knowledge before risking passengers.
Mara, carrierKeeps a careful list of everyone stranded across the river.Wants people and goods recovered; can pay the promised 80 coins, not an unlimited ransom.
Brin, toll thiefSpeaks confidently until asked who issued the quarantine.Wants supplies and escape; will abandon the toll if exposed with a safe way to leave.
Nera, salvagerRings the bell with a broken spar and shouts between peals.Wants Tovin rescued; can describe the sentries' boundary.
Tovin, salvagerHides beneath empty sacks, clutching the station's keeper log.Wants a safe route out; knows the west service hatch avoids the threshold.

None of these people needs to become a fight merely because the heroes distrust them. If a consequential NPC-only action needs a roll, use the ordinary NPC procedure; Oren's description does not grant an unprinted combat ability.

Routes at a glance

FromToRoute and information
Ferry shelterToll yardA visible causeway; the crew can see travelers approaching.
Ferry shelterFar landingOren's boat, once convinced; no automatic travel roll on calm water.
CausewayWest service hatchA bank path found by examining the old maintenance marker; reeds conceal it from the yard.
Toll yardBell loftExterior stairs; the crew avoids the loft because of the noise below.
Far landingSignal room entranceA short stone passage ending at a clearly painted boundary.
Service hatchStores alcoveA cramped but passable maintenance corridor, outside the sentries' assigned boundary.
Bell loftSignal room entranceInterior stairs; Nera can warn approaching heroes from above.

Use ordinary travel narration between these nearby places unless pursuit or another immediate danger makes movement order important. No route is secretly impassable just because it avoids a prepared encounter.

1. The ferry shelter

Describe a rain-dark roof, travelers sharing a small fire, and the bell beyond the mist. Give the players Mara's offer and Oren's explanation. Examining the signal chart nailed beside his door reveals that repeated paired strokes request rescue. The present strokes are broken by long pauses, not a quarantine signal.

Oren will lend the boat and guide the crossing if the heroes show him a credible plan for checking the landing. He can be convinced by the chart and a proposal to approach away from the yard; a roll is unnecessary once his concern is answered. An uncertain attempt to persuade him to row straight into danger uses the social procedure, with its stakes agreed first. Taking the boat without consent changes his relationship to the party rather than automatically starting a battle.

The maintenance marker on the causeway map is visible to anyone who examines it. Oren remembers that workers once used a path beneath the western bank. This gives the party another route even if nobody can negotiate boat passage.

2. The false toll

Use @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.da-rules.JournalEntry.fcfeb03f877503a3.JournalEntryPage.95ce2be216cc6e84]{three Road Bandits} and @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.da-rules.JournalEntry.fcfeb03f877503a3.JournalEntryPage.0fb696c4bf5836aa]{one Bandit Bow}, CV 37 total. Brin uses one Road Bandit card, with no additional leader actions.

For a grid, draw a yard 12 squares wide and 10 deep. The causeway enters at the south; the loft stairs and landing exit are north. A cart across the center leaves a two-square passage on either side. Two waist-high stone remnants provide heavy cover where a narrow attack path remains; they do not make targets invisible. Give the bow a position behind one wall, not an inaccessible firing platform. The western bank path remains an exit. Draw these features before a fight starts.

Brin demands 10 coins per traveler but accepts a credible alternative that gets the crew away with supplies. The heroes can challenge the quarantine using the bell chart, talk to individual crew members, pay, bypass the yard, or fight. A visibly forged notice carries no official seal; inspecting it reveals this without a roll. Exposure makes Brin willing to leave if the heroes allow escape.

If violence starts, the crew uses its printed attacks and maneuvers. They have no surprise turn, free opening volley or automatic disarm. Follow the normal initiative procedure. When Brin falls or two crew members are out of the fight, the others try to withdraw or surrender. That is their chosen response to danger, not a new morale roll. Their lethal attacks remain lethal; a surrender must happen before 0 HP if they are to survive without an explicit exception.

The crew does not pursue through the signal room. Allow the heroes to learn that boundary by watching or talking to them. If the crew escapes, it does not immediately return fully healed as an unbudgeted second wave.

3. The bell loft

Nera has wedged the inner stair door shut. She lowers a rope when the heroes make contact and can unbar the exterior door once they reach the stairs. No roll is needed for her to admit obvious rescuers after they speak.

She explains that the sentries stopped when she fled beyond the painted line. She has not seen Tovin leave the stores. She will accompany a careful rescue but has no special combat actions. Her broken bell spar explains the irregular signal. Fixing it or giving her a suitable tool lets her ring the correct signal without requiring a crafting recipe for an ordinary improvised handle.

4. The service hatch

Mud has swollen the hatch against its frame. A safe, unhurried approach with suitable leverage opens it after a few minutes without a roll. If the bandits are following, announce that three heroes can reach it, with one binary group attempt, target 7, before their pursuers arrive. Each contributes a Brawn result. Below 7, the hatch stays closed and the pursuers arrive; do not add damage that was never at stake.

This group procedure is outside combat. If combat has already begun, each hero must use their own permitted action instead; do not import the group attempt into the turn order. The heroes may still negotiate, retreat or use another route.

Beyond the hatch, Tovin can crawl out of the alcove without crossing the sentries' boundary. He brings the keeper log. It contains a sketch of the threshold and the old instruction to deny passage into the signal room. Reading it requires no identification spell. It does not grant a command over arbitrary undead.

5. The painted threshold

Use @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.da-rules.JournalEntry.fcfeb03f877503a3.JournalEntryPage.01ba5c11f1e1392d]{three Skeleton Sentries}, CV 24 total. Their bodies and swords are visible through the entrance. Dry clicking begins when someone approaches. A faded red stripe crosses the floor. One sentry steps forward as a stick or other object passes over the stripe, then returns to its post when the object is withdrawn. Show this warning before an unaware character crosses.

Draw an 8-by-8-square chamber, with a two-square entrance at the south, the stores corridor outside its western wall, and an old signal mechanism against the north wall. Broken benches form two patches of difficult terrain. The guardians remain inside their assigned room. They are not standing shoulder to shoulder in a one-square entrance that prevents every alternative approach.

The rescue and reopening of the ordinary landing do not require entry. Tovin's route and Nera's stairs remain outside the boundary. The heroes may secure the outer door and warn future workers, leaving the guardians in place. Fighting is an option if the party wants to clear the chamber, not a hidden condition of Mara's payment. The guardians have no additional reinforcements or powers.

If the party fights here immediately after the toll yard without a safe breath, consider the accumulated pressure. Do not call the pair of encounters a single standard fight just because each total is below 40. Both rosters and all expended resources belong in the session's record.

Clues that prevent a dead end

Necessary understandingWays to learn it
The bell is a rescue request, not proof of plagueOren's memory; his chart; speaking with Nera.
There is a route around the toll yardThe shelter's map; the visible maintenance marker; Oren's account.
The sentries guard a boundaryNera's account; observing the threshold; the keeper log.
Tovin can leave without fighting the sentriesThe service route; Nera's description of the alcove; Tovin answering a call.

If the heroes call out from a safe place, let survivors answer when they can hear. The adventure does not require the players to discover every clue or enter every room.

If the heroes delay

At dusk, Brin's crew intends to leave with what it has collected. Tell the heroes about their packed bags and arguments over departure. Unless the heroes intervene, the crew departs along the causeway; it does not murder the workers off-screen to force urgency. Nera stops ringing when exhausted and takes shelter in the loft. The quiet bell then means the signal stopped, not automatic proof that she died. The sentries maintain their boundary.

These developments change information and opportunities without forcing a prescribed ending. Change their timing if the opening occurs at another hour, and communicate the signs before a decision depends on them.

Rewards and aftermath

Mara pays the 80-coin company reward when the survivors are out and safe access is restored. With four heroes, an equal share is 20 each. The rescued workers offer a Rope Coil and Lever and Wedges, worth 5 coins each, from their own supplies. These are physical items with normal Bulk, not new abilities. The party may decline them or return them after the work. Intact recovered enemy gear uses normal resale and trade; do not award its sale price as coins as well as handing over the gear.

No reward requires killing the bandits or skeletons. Oren remembers who helped, and the keeper log may point to another station whose lamp still burns. If you choose this rescue as a level milestone, award it for resolving the adventure, not for clearing every creature from the map. Level advancement remains the DA's decision, not an automatic rule attached to this example.

Places and People

Heroes of Legend · Dungeon Architect’s Guide & Bestiary

A settlement becomes memorable when the heroes have a reason to return. Perhaps the innkeeper knows their names, a workshop holds an unfinished commission, or a friend waits for news. You can build that connection with a few people and places before you know the region's ancient history.

HOL does not require a particular world. Decide with your group what magic looks like, how distant communities exchange news, and which powers shape local life. Keep those choices separate from rules that apply to every character.

Begin within reach

Choose a home base, a nearby danger and a route between them. Add one person who needs the heroes, one who can help them, and one whose interests may conflict with theirs. Name the next destination only when it becomes useful.

Give each location an ordinary purpose. A ruin once stored grain, held prisoners, watched a road or honored the dead. That purpose suggests entrances, rooms, tools and paths. Its current inhabitants then change it. A flooded granary becomes a fungus garden; a beacon tower becomes a smuggler's signal post.

Location promptQuestions that make it playable
A settlementWhat brings people here? What do they need from elsewhere? Who settles disputes?
A routeWho travels it? What can be seen ahead? Where can travelers leave it?
A ruinWhat was it built to do? What still works? Who now claims it?
A lairHow does its inhabitant enter, feed and escape? What warns an approaching visitor?
A refugeWho offers shelter? What makes it safe now? What responsibilities accompany hospitality?

Draw for decisions

On a regional map, show routes, obstacles and recognizable landmarks. Exact miles are unnecessary when they do not affect a choice. If two routes differ in travel time, explain that difference along with what the heroes know about their risks. Ordinary travel does not require routine rolls or an exhaustion track.

On a tactical map, use squares. Mark difficult terrain, actual barriers, attack paths and usable exits. Partial obstruction applies 1 Bane; heavy cover with a narrow attack path applies 3. An unseen target behind an opaque barrier is not merely a heavily covered target. Abilities still require their own targeting conditions.

Give melee heroes approaches, ranged heroes sight lines, and movement abilities places to matter. Avoid filling every battlefield with the same waist-high walls. A bridge, orchard, crowded workshop and wind-scoured roof should suggest different choices before a creature takes its first turn.

> Example: the working mill. The yard offers open movement. Sacks inside create > difficult terrain; the mill wall blocks sight entirely. A doorway provides an > attack path only where a target is visible through it. The wheel is machinery, > not automatically an extra creature with a turn. If it presents a hazard, define > that hazard's trigger and resolution before someone risks it.

People you can portray quickly

Write four things for an important NPC: a recognizable detail, a current want, a useful piece of knowledge, and a boundary they hesitate to cross. Add a name and one relationship. You now have enough to answer most questions naturally.

NPCAt the tableWhat changes their mind
A keeper of a roadside shrineRepairs travelers' straps while listening; wants the road safe.A practical plan for the missing pilgrims matters more than flattery.
A quarry foremanDust in every seam; knows where the newest tunnel broke through.Will stop work if shown a real danger, but needs a way to pay the crew.
A local brokerRemembers favors precisely; knows which goods are scarce.Accepts a useful introduction or an agreed trade, not imaginary coin value.
A young watch officerRehearses orders under their breath; fears being blamed.Written evidence or a respected witness may resolve their uncertainty.

These descriptions do not grant abilities, resistances or skill modifiers. If an NPC needs a combat role, select a fitting existing creature card and describe the person around it. If their important noncombat task needs mechanics, record its attribute and applicable capability openly rather than inventing a hidden unbeatable score after the player acts.

Factions with room to change

A faction needs a shared purpose and a means to pursue it. Write what it wants, what it can offer, what it can threaten, and where its members disagree. Rivalry becomes interesting when the heroes can affect it.

Consider two groups competing over a flooded quarry. Workers want safe access and paid wages. A shrine's custodians want the newly exposed burial chamber left undisturbed. Both may oppose a merchant who hides evidence of the breach. The heroes can help several people without accepting every demand from any one group.

Keep a short record of what each group learns about the heroes. Information must travel. A distant faction does not automatically know a private decision made in a sealed room. If a messenger carries the news, that person becomes a useful part of the adventure.

Cultures without cages

Culture describes learned customs and community experience; ancestry does not force one culture, profession or loyalty. Let towns contain disagreement and travelers carry habits from elsewhere. Ask players how their own origins fit rather than assigning a personality from a character option.

Likewise, a deity, spirit or tradition can have a local name without changing a card's action or healing cost. A priest and a scholar may describe Life energy differently while using the same underlying rules. If you want a setting choice to change a rule, discuss that change explicitly before character choices depend on it.

Let places remember

After an adventure, change a few visible details. The damaged bridge gains a new rail. A market stall sells charms shaped like the creature the heroes drove away. A family leaves a chair empty for someone who did not return. These signs make choices matter without needing a regional simulation.

Return to people as their wants change. An employer may become a partner, a rescued stranger a critic, a frightened rival a dependable guide. Keep their earlier actions in view so the relationship grows from play rather than replacing itself each visit.

Give languages places to live. A river port may speak three, while a remote valley uses a local language and a handful of trade phrases. An old bridge may carry a warning in a language nobody nearby reads. These details invite the heroes to listen, find help and form relationships.

Use the shared language list as a ready starting point. You do not need to invent a family tree of every language before the first session. Decide what the party shares, which communities they are likely to meet, and one unfamiliar language that can matter to an early adventure.

Set expectations before creation

Tell players which name replaces Common, which ordinary choices are useful near the starting location, and whether any normally uncommon language is ordinary in this campaign. A port where dragons trade openly might make Draconic ordinary; an isolated kingdom might have no living speakers of it. Explain that difference before someone spends a language grant.

The starting baseline is Common plus one ordinary home language, with explicit extra grants added afterward. If your world uses a different baseline, agree on it before creation and preserve meaningful choices from language-granting traits. Do not invalidate a selected language merely because the first prepared adventure uses another one. Give its speakers, documents or contacts a place in the campaign.

Language follows upbringing and experience. A dwarf raised in an elven community can speak Elven; a human scholar can know Dwarven. A culture entry is a way of life, not a single nation with one compulsory language. Deep Halls might use Dwarven, a regional language or several languages in different settlements.

Add or replace a language

Write a short entry with the following information. Keep this record beside your campaign notes and share the player-relevant choices before they become purchases.

RecordDecide
Name and scopeOne language, not every language of a species or continent.
Speakers and placesWho uses it, where they learned it, and whom they trade with.
AvailabilityOrdinary or uncommon in this campaign; which existing grants can choose it.
Form and scriptSpoken, signed or another explicit form; whether it has writing and what is needed to use it.
Related varietiesWhich dialects are mutually understood, and which are separate languages.
Adventure useOne conversation, document, contact or discovery that rewards knowing it.

Do not give a language an inherent Boon to persuasion or a damage bonus. Its value is access to people and meaning. If you want a magical language that compels a listener or opens a sealed gate, put that supernatural effect in an ability, item or specific adventure feature with its own rules.

> Example: Reed Speech. The fishing communities of the southern marsh use an > ordinary spoken language written on split reed strips. Neighboring village > dialects are mutually understood. A lost island dialect is not automatically a > separate choice: decide whether it is still understandable before preparing a > translation obstacle. A ferryman's account in Reed Speech reveals which boat > crossed after sunset. Nothing about the language requires its speakers to share > ancestry or allegiance.

Use barriers to create choices

An unfamiliar language should suggest a next step. The party might hire an interpreter, visit a shrine's archive, find a bilingual inscription or use Translate the Fragment. Let the players choose which cost or relationship to accept. A necessary clue should have another way forward if nobody chose its language. The specialist can obtain a clearer, faster or richer answer without making the rest of the adventure depend on one choice made at creation.

Do not call for a roll just to understand ordinary speech in a known language. If the uncertainty concerns a damaged inscription, a lie or a coded message, name that problem and its consequences. A Knowledge roll does not confer an unknown language. Where a task supports progress, use the existing procedure and the applicable card rather than inventing a separate translation die.

An interpreter has knowledge, motives and limits like any other person. Establish what they can actually translate. Routine honest interpretation needs no second roll for every sentence. If deception or misunderstanding matters, show evidence and use the normal player-roll rules. Never replace a card's explicit shared-language requirement with an unannounced exception.

Treat dialects as mutually understandable unless a meaningful setting distinction was established. A strange accent is usually flavor. Signed languages are complete languages, not a bundle of secret combat signals: they require visible gestures and follow the same rules for understanding. Ordinary gestures remain available to everyone for simple meanings.

Read the bestiary's communication line

The communication line states what that creature can do. “Understands” does not mean “speaks.” “None” does not mean it fails to react to posture, food or danger; it means the card grants no linguistic communication. A creature's ability to communicate also does not guarantee its willingness to negotiate.

Existing entryPrepare it for your world
Common and its community's languageName one local language before play. Goblin, Orc or Kobold may fit, but community matters more than ancestry.
Court, regional or scholarly languageSelect one actual language from your campaign; these are not grants of every language in that category.
Sacred languages or language of its oathName the languages tied to that being's tradition. Celestial is one possible choice, not a compulsory one.
Old woodland speechUse Elven or Fey, or name a distinct local language and decide its availability.
Languages known in lifeChoose the dead person's languages. Being undead grants no universal language of the dead.
Maker's languageName the maker's language and retain any “understands” or “repeats” limitation.
Images, calls, gestures or lightConvey only the meanings the card allows; do not silently add speech, mind-reading or perfect translation.

Record concrete choices beside the creature entry in your adventure notes. When several creatures share a community, reuse that choice consistently. Summoned forms retain their printed communication, but commands follow the summon rules: an uncommanded summon does nothing. Language never supplies free commands or extra actions.

Learning during a campaign

Honor permanent language grants already printed on a trait or ability. For another route to fluency, agree on its source and cost before the hero commits resources. The core catalog currently has no universal Language Study purchase or fixed training calendar. Do not disguise either as an existing rule. You can introduce a clearly described campaign option or grant, but distinguish it from a translation, a tutor's service or a temporary magical effect.

Keep the reward visible. A letter understood, a name pronounced correctly or a conversation without an intermediary can show the benefit more clearly than an extra modifier. Languages give your world voices; the rules need only make those voices usable at the table.

Building Encounters

Heroes of Legend · Dungeon Architect’s Guide & Bestiary

An encounter asks the heroes to make a consequential choice. A fight might decide who holds a bridge, whether a prisoner escapes, or how much danger the company accepts to recover a lost object. Begin with that purpose. Then choose creatures and a place that make the decision interesting.

Combat Value, or CV, helps compare creatures and assemble an initial roster. It does not account perfectly for a particular party, map or combination of abilities. The budgets in this chapter are playtest starting points. They have not yet been calibrated to promise a particular fight length or chance of injury.

Prepare the encounter in six decisions

1. Choose the objective. What do the heroes want, and what does the opposition want? 2. Review the party. Note actual levels, attack options, healing, control, mobility, supplies, wounds and available Grit. 3. Choose an initial CV budget. Account for party size, level and intended danger. 4. Select a roster. Give its members useful roles and understandable reasons to act. 5. Draw the relevant terrain. Show approaches, exits, sight lines and hazards. 6. Decide what can end the encounter. Include retreat, surrender or a completed objective where the situation allows them.

Write down all creatures that may join before the heroes can safely recover. A reinforcement wave is part of the danger, even if it begins off the map.

Starting budgets

For four heroes of the same level, the current standard seed is 32 + 8 × level. Use the row below as a first estimate, then examine the actual matchup.

For N same-level heroes, multiply the four-hero budget by N ÷ 4, then by the difficulty multiplier. Round the final result to a convenient whole CV.

> Example: a smaller company. Three level-1 heroes have an initial standard > budget of 40 × 3 ÷ 4 = 30 CV. Five level-1 heroes have 50 CV. A hard > encounter for those five starts at 50 × 1.5 = 75 CV.

> Example: experienced companions. Heroes at levels 1, 1, 3 and 3 contribute > 10 + 10 + 14 + 14 = 48 CV before difficulty. A hard seed is 72. Review the > lower-level heroes' vulnerability separately; the total does not protect them > from an attack designed to pressure the stronger members.

A roster need not equal the budget exactly. A sensible 36-CV scene is more useful than an unrelated extra creature added merely to reach 40.

Give each creature a job

Start with a few creatures whose actions you can run confidently. Three to five enemies make a useful first test against four heroes. Their roles should help you choose actions, not grant unprinted bonuses.

Role in this encounterWhat to look for on its cardA decision it creates
Hold a routeResistance, Defend, suitable positioningGo around, displace it, or commit attacks?
Pressure from rangeA printed ranged action and a usable sight lineTake cover or close the distance?
Separate companionsPush, pull, mobility or grapplingRecover formation or exploit another opening?
Disrupt a planA printed condition or interference abilityProtect the affected ally or remove the source?
Sustain alliesA printed healing ability with its costPressure the healer or overwhelm another target?
Protect an objectiveMotive and terrain that reward staying nearbyFight it directly or complete the task elsewhere?

Begin by adding one unusual capability at a time. Several enemies that repeatedly apply Dazed or Paralyzed can create a scene in which players spend much of their time unable to participate. Test that combination deliberately before presenting it as an ordinary fight.

A creature with several attacks chooses among them using its normal action budget. A claw and a bite do not grant two Main Actions. A solo has one turn and one Reaction; there are no automatic legendary turns. Objectives and terrain can make a solo memorable, but they do not secretly supply extra actions. Any additional creatures contribute their own CV.

Terrain changes the matchup

A ranged enemy in an unreachable position can be far more dangerous than the same enemy in a room with several approaches. A narrow doorway can prevent the heroes from using their numbers. A deep drop can turn modest forced movement into the most important part of an attack.

Inspect the map from the players' side. Can they reach the enemy? Can they see it? Can they retreat? Can an ally get beside someone who needs stabilization? Does a large creature fit through the route you expect it to use? Check its actual footprint, not just the miniature you happen to own.

Show meaningful features before the choice that depends on them. A ledge can be dangerous without being hidden. A loose bridge rail should look loose. If a damaging hazard operates during combat, record its additional pressure separately; the creature budget does not already include it.

Five encounters to begin with

These scenes use current creature CVs. Each presents a motive and a route to an outcome other than defeating every enemy. Their totals are examples, not certified encounter ratings.

The false toll. A cart blocks the road, but its axle is sound. The robbers want supplies without a dangerous fight. Put the bow where heroes can reach or outflank it. Inspecting the supposed breakdown exposes the lie; negotiation, an alternate route or a forceful advance can settle the scene. The full crossing adventure provides a worked version.

The opened barrow. The guardians repeat an old boundary command. A stolen burial token explains why the entrance has become dangerous; returning it can settle this particular disturbance if you establish that relationship in the adventure. That is local story context, not a universal skeleton weakness. Leave room around the entry so the encounter does not become a one-square queue.

Tracks around the camp. The camp obstructs the pack's route to its den. Tracks and anxious circling reveal the problem. The wolves use their printed pack ability against isolated prey. Moving camp or clearing a passage may prevent the fight. Do not grant every animal in the bestiary the same pack ability.

The bridge has an owner. The troll and robbers share an uneasy toll arrangement. Food, tribute or turning them against one another may open the way. Show the drop and the troll's push capability through signs or observation before the party commits. Fire counterplay can change the fight substantially; the 43-CV total does not price a lethal fall or inaccessible firing position.

The watch will not stand down. Soldiers believe the cultist has lawful orders. A forged seal, an inconsistent instruction or a credible witness can break that belief. If a fight occurs, track the soldiers' separate Defend and Shield Hunker costs and durations. Their layered defenses can make this harder for some parties than its total suggests.

Healing, flight and summoned allies

Healing follows the same rules for players and ordinary NPCs. A healer pays the printed HP cost before resolution and must remain above 0. Free hands, range, actions, Life resistance and opportunity attacks matter. Give the party visible information about enemy healing rather than silently increasing its cost or limiting it to a number of uses.

A flying creature needs the flight actually printed on its card. Review its ability to attack while staying out of reach and what the party can do about that. Do not assume every party has a ranged solution because bows exist in the equipment list. Place cover, objectives or approaches that make the encounter playable, or present the creature as a danger to avoid until prepared.

Summons consume their controller's commands. An uncommanded summon does nothing; it does not provide a free guard, scout or opportunity attack. Its six-square tether, inability to receive healing and disappearance when its controller falls all affect its usefulness. Count what it can actually do, not an imaginary independent turn. Do not automatically increase the budget to erase a summoner's investment.

Observe, then adjust the estimate

For playtests, record the actual party and supplies rather than an idealized average hero. Note rounds, healing actions and HP costs, Grit spent, new wounds, depleted supplies, escapes, disabled turns, and whether players discovered the intended counterplay. Record whether the encounter was enjoyable as well as whether the company survived.

The design targets are roughly four rounds for a typical encounter, six for a hard one and ten for an extreme one. A reasonably prepared party's typical encounter is intended to have about a 20–30% chance of at least one new wound without a healer, or 5–15% with one. These are goals across many trials, not requirements for an individual table or evidence that this budget achieves them.

If an encounter disappoints, identify the cause before changing all its numbers. Was the enemy unreachable? Did the party overlook a capability because it was unclear? Did control remove too many turns? Did both sides spend their time healing? Revise the relevant part and test again. Preserve what made the encounter memorable.

Hazards, Traps and Environmental Challenges

Heroes of Legend · Dungeon Architect’s Guide & Bestiary

A chain clicks inside the wall. Hot air escapes between the stones. A newly repaired board stands out from the older floor. A good hazard gives the heroes something to notice, a consequence to understand, and more than one way to respond.

Use existing actions, attributes, conditions and progress rules to resolve these challenges. A trap does not need a second difficulty system. A hazardous place does not need a combat turn merely because it can hurt someone.

The example hazards below have their own damage, targets, areas and timings. These are not universal trap damage or calibrated additions to encounter CV.

Write a hazard for use

FieldWhat to record
SignsWhat can be seen, heard, smelled or learned before contact?
Trigger and areaWhat activates it, and which creatures or squares are affected?
ResolutionIs there a roll? Which attribute? What does each outcome do?
Timing and repetitionDoes it happen once, repeat on a stated event, or continue until stopped?
CounterplayHow can the heroes avoid, interrupt or remove it?
AftermathWhat conditions, damage or changed terrain remain?

An attack-like hazard uses player defense outcomes: Weak is the most dangerous, Strong the least. Each affected player rolls for an area hazard. An active attempt to repair or disable something instead uses the acting character's attribute and progress. Label the distinction. Do not describe a successful defense and then accidentally read the Strong attack damage against it.

Describe visible signs freely. If players expose the mechanism by lifting its cover, show it. Ask for Reason when a search is uncertain and has a consequence, not as a toll on every useful observation. Specialized abilities retain their printed advantages; ordinary inspection does not acquire all their outcomes.

Spring spear

A polished scuff cuts across the dust before a narrow doorway. A dark slot in the jamb is exactly the height of an unwary traveler's ribs.

Trigger and area: weight on the marked threshold releases one spear into its one-square space. A creature crossing without avoiding or disabling the plate is the target. If several cross, only the first activation fires the loaded spear.

Resolution: Agility defense; no inherent Boons or Banes. Deal physical damage according to the defense result.

Weak defenseStandard defenseStrong defense
5 physical3 physical1 physical

Timing: one discharge. Someone must physically reload and reset the mechanism before it can fire again; it does not reload itself each round.

Counterplay: the plate can be stepped over or avoided with a legal route once noticed. An exposed catch can be wedged safely when there is time and access. If a hero must reach it while under immediate pressure, use a Main Action and an Agility roll: Weak holds the catch only while the hero stays and holds it; Standard wedges it for passage; Strong also leaves it easy to release deliberately. Explain these stakes before the attempt. A suitable specialist card may provide its own method.

Aftermath: the discharged spear and slot are obvious. No lingering Bleeding is added unless an explicit effect applies it. Do not erase the party's work by resetting the trap when they return.

Furnace vent

A red glow pulses beneath the grate. Its shutter hangs open, and the release lever shudders with every breath of the bellows.

Trigger and area: operating the bellows while the shutter is open releases a burst into the three consecutive squares directly in front of the grate. Mark those squares visibly. The bellows requires someone to operate it; this entry adds no automatic hazard turn.

Resolution: each exposed player rolls Agility defense; no inherent modifiers. The table shows complete outcomes.

Weak defenseStandard defenseStrong defense
3 Fire and Burning 22 Fire and Burning 11 Fire

Timing: resolve a burst when the bellows is operated. In combat, operating it requires a Main Action by someone who can reach its handle. Characters can see and interrupt an operator through their ordinary abilities; operating machinery is not automatically a new opportunity-attack trigger.

Counterplay: leave the marked squares, stop the operator, or close the adjacent release lever with a Maneuver and no roll. A closed shutter prevents further bursts until someone reopens it with a Maneuver. Clearly visible controls offer an immediate useful choice.

Aftermath: existing Burning resolves and decays normally even after the shutter closes. A plausible Main Action can reduce it by 1. Closing the vent does not itself heal damage or remove Burning. Include the vent's possible pressure when evaluating any combat fought here; its CV has not been established.

Sluice gate

The gate's chain jumps with every surge. Water carries leaves through the open channel, tracing a straight path toward a stone catch basin.

Trigger and area: opening the gate releases one surge along a marked line of six channel squares, one square wide. It affects creatures in those squares at that instant; this is not a persistent aura or an attack on everyone who enters later.

Resolution: Agility defense, no inherent modifiers. Each affected player rolls.

Weak defenseStandard defenseStrong defense
Push 3 downstreamPush 2 downstreamPush 1 downstream

Timing: one surge per filled reservoir. The reservoir takes an hour to refill; there is no second surge during the same combat. The gate can be opened by an adjacent Main Action without a roll.

Counterplay: stand on the raised walkway outside the channel, close the gate before it releases, or interrupt the operator with an applicable ability. The gate cannot be closed retroactively after the surge resolves. A ready escape route should be visible before someone steps into the channel.

Aftermath: apply Stability and terrain costs normally. This entry deals no direct damage, but collisions along its forced path use the ordinary collision rules. The catch basin has a flat floor at the channel's level, not an unannounced lethal drop. If you place a drop there, describe and evaluate that additional danger.

The whispering inscription

Words drift at the edge of the reader's attention. For a moment, every nearby voice sounds like their own, speaking half a sentence too late.

Trigger and area: a creature deliberately reads the exposed inscription within one square. Merely seeing the stone from a distance does not activate it. Warn the players with its audible echoes and the writer's nearby note, “Cover before copying.”

Resolution: Reason defense, no inherent modifiers.

Weak defenseStandard defenseStrong defense
Dazed 2Dazed 1No condition

Timing: once per reader during the scene. Looking away and back does not repeat it. This scene limit belongs to this inscription, not to every magical hazard.

Counterplay: cover the writing without reading it, turn the tablet face down, or use a suitable identification ability from a permitted position to learn its properties. This is an object with a specific effect, not permission to invent a generic counterspell roll. Reading it is optional; do not place the adventure's only essential clue behind an unavoidable activation.

Aftermath: Dazed affects action-category selection at the start of the affected turn and decays at its end. It does not undo spent actions. In a safe scene, allow the temporary distraction to pass; do not inflict permanent mental scars merely because its description is unsettling.

A blocked escape

Fresh rubble fills the service passage. Dust still falls from a timber that is bending under the stones.

This is an obstacle, not an automatic damaging trap. State whether the heroes have time to clear it safely. With adequate time, tools and no danger, describe the work. Under pressure, declare its progress target and what another attempt will cost.

Example configuration: outside combat, up to three heroes can work abreast. Clearing a passage is cumulative, target 8, one minute per attempt. Each contributing Brawn roll adds 1/2/3 progress. If pursuing guards will arrive in two minutes, announce the warning before the first attempt. Weak, Standard and Strong add 6; a later Weak and Weak add the remaining 2. The party must still decide who watches the route.

A supported alternate path or a card that changes the obstruction can provide a different solution. During combat, use individual actions such as Force; no group check is available. Do not add a collapsing-ceiling damage roll unless that danger was separately established.

Travel, water and heights

Use weather and terrain to create choices. A flooded ford can make the longer bridge route attractive. A storm may make arrival before dark uncertain. Tell the players the consequences of each known route; do not demand a travel roll simply because another day passes.

Climbing and swimming normally cost two movement per square. This assumes the surface or water is traversable. Specialist cards may improve what the hero can do. Safe jumps within the ordinary Agility-based limits need no roll. Risky execution can call for Agility after you establish what is at stake.

Falling uses the existing rate of 3 HP per two squares fallen. Do not conceal a fall's height until after a hero jumps. Resolve exceptional surfaces and landing circumstances openly; a hazard entry should state any specific additional condition rather than assuming every fall applies Prone or a wound.

Hazards during combat

Before initiative, identify a hazard's trigger, affected area, frequency and the cost of operating or disabling it. If it repeats, write down exactly when. Do not quietly give it a full creature turn, an opportunity attack or a new CV because it sits on a battle map.

A creature that knows a trap can try to use its terrain and controls within its normal actions. That knowledge does not automatically make it immune. Players who learn the same mechanism should be able to exploit it under the same procedure.

After play, record which hazards created useful decisions and which merely added bookkeeping. Remove repeated rolls that do not change the situation. A danger the heroes recognize and cleverly avoid has done its job.

Treasure and Rewards

Heroes of Legend · Dungeon Architect’s Guide & Bestiary

A reward gives the heroes another choice. Coins can buy passage or supplies. A recipe can turn future ingredients into something useful. An introduction can open a door that no weapon would open safely. Choose rewards that make the next adventure more interesting and acknowledge what the company accomplished.

Use the @UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.895ef20bc4923b2e.JournalEntryPage.cfa94361944ba875]{ordinary market} as the common price reference. HOL uses coins, with no metal denominations. Prices do not increase merely because a hero gains a level.

Begin with useful scale

A simple meal costs 1 coin and a plain bed costs 2 per night, meals separate. A Rope Coil costs 5; an ordinary melee weapon costs 12; a Lesser Healing Bottle costs 20. These anchors help you describe what a reward means to people in the world.

There is no established mandatory treasure total per level in this manuscript. Consider the party's current supplies, actual needs and opportunities to spend. A reward can be generous without buying a new discipline rank: coins purchase objects and services, while DP purchases character development.
